Front: Who created the first periodic table, and when?
Back: Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869. He arranged elements on cards by atomic mass and even left blank spaces for elements that hadn't been discovered yet!
A regular, repeated pattern — just like a calendar repeats days into weeks, the periodic table repeats patterns in element properties.

Front: What are the 3 particles inside an atom?
Back:
* Protons — positive charge, inside the nucleus
* Neutrons — no charge, inside the nucleus
* Electrons — negative charge, buzzing around outside the nucleus
The number of protons in an atom. This is what makes each element unique!
The average mass of an element's atoms, measured in atomic mass units (amu).

Front: What 4 things does each square on the periodic table tell you?
Back:
* Atomic number (top)
* Chemical symbol (middle) — 1 or 2 letters like Fe for iron
* Element name (below symbol)
* Atomic mass (bottom)

Front: What is a group (family) on the periodic table?
Back: A vertical column (up and down). There are 18 groups. Elements in the same group have similar properties!

Front: What is a period on the periodic table?
Back: A horizontal row (left to right). There are 7 periods. Properties gradually change as you move across a period.

Front: What are valence electrons and why do they matter?
Back: The electrons in the outermost shell of an atom. They are the ones involved in chemical reactions. Elements in the same group have the same number of valence electrons — that's why they behave similarly!

Front: How many valence electrons do Group 1 and Group 18 elements have?
Back:
Group 1 = 1 valence electron
Group 18 = 8 valence electrons

Front: Where are metals found on the periodic table?
Back: To the LEFT of the zigzag line. Most elements on the table are metals!

* Shiny (luster)
* Malleable — can be pounded into shapes
* Ductile — can be pulled into wire
* Good conductors of heat and electricity
A material that can be hammered or pounded into different shapes without breaking. Example: hammering gold into jewelry.
A material that can be pulled or stretched into a thin wire. Example: copper wire.
How easily an element combines (reacts) with other elements. Sodium is very reactive (explodes in water!). Gold is very unreactive (stays shiny forever).
When a metal slowly reacts with oxygen in the air and breaks down. Example: rust on iron.

The MOST reactive metals.
* Never found pure in nature
* So soft you can cut them with a plastic knife
* Examples: sodium (Na) and potassium (K)
* Sodium is in table salt, potassium is in bananas

Reactive but not as much as Group 1.
* Hard, gray-white, good conductors
* Examples: magnesium (Mg) and calcium (Ca)
* Calcium is in bones, teeth, milk, and leafy veggies

The familiar metals: iron, copper, nickel, silver, gold.
* Hard and shiny
* Good conductors of electricity
* Less reactive than Groups 1 and 2
* Used to make colorful paints
A mixture of two or more metals that combines the best properties of each.

Front: Name 4 common alloys and what they're made of.
Back:
* Steel = iron + carbon (buildings, cars)
* Bronze = copper + tin (statues)
* Brass = copper + zinc
* Stainless steel = iron + carbon + chromium + vanadium (won't rust!)

Front: Which metal is a liquid at room temperature?
Back: Mercury (Hg) — the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

Front: Where are nonmetals found on the periodic table?
Back: To the RIGHT of the zigzag line.

* Dull (not shiny)
* Brittle — break or crumble instead of bending
* Poor conductors of heat and electricity
* Many are gases at room temperature

Front: What is special about the carbon family (Group 14)?
Back: Carbon is the key element of life — ALL living things contain carbon. Scientists have found over a billion carbon compounds!

Front: What percentage of the atmosphere is nitrogen?
Back: Almost 80%! Nitrogen doesn't react easily with other elements. Plants need it to grow, which is why farmers use fertilizers.

Front: Name 3 facts about the oxygen family (Group 16).
Back:
* Oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust
* Your blood carries oxygen to every part of your body
* Ozone (O3) protects us from the sun's harmful UV rays
* Sulfur has a rotten-egg smell

Very reactive nonmetals.
* Fluorine — most reactive nonmetal (in toothpaste)
* Chlorine — in table salt and pools
* Bromine — photographic film
* Iodine — antiseptic for cuts

The LEAST reactive elements — they almost never combine with anything because they already have 8 valence electrons.
* Helium — balloons
* Neon — glowing signs
* Most weren't discovered until the late 1800s

Front: Why are noble gases so unreactive?
Back: They already have 8 valence electrons (a full outer shell), so they don't need to gain, lose, or share electrons. They're already 'happy'!

* Sits alone in the top left corner
* Simplest element — just 1 proton and 1 electron
* Makes up over 90% of atoms in the universe
* Usually found combined with oxygen in water (H2O)
Elements found along the zigzag line that have properties of BOTH metals and nonmetals. The most common is silicon (Si), used in sand, glass, cement, and computer chips.
A material that can sometimes conduct electricity and sometimes can't. Silicon and germanium are semiconductors used to make computer chips, transistors, and lasers.
A material that carries heat or electricity well. Most metals are good conductors.

Front: What is table salt made of?
Back: Sodium (Na) — a metal that explodes in water — and chlorine (Cl) — a poisonous gas. But together as NaCl, they're totally safe to eat!

Two rows at the BOTTOM of the periodic table, also called rare earth elements.
* Only thorium (Th) and uranium (U) exist naturally
* Elements after uranium were made in labs and some last only a fraction of a second
